source.title: Muon Optimizer Accelerates Grokking
source.authors: Amund Tveit; Bjørn G. Remseth; A. Skogvold

record.tranche_reason: Tests delayed generalization on small algorithmic tasks and compares its timing under different optimizers, using a modern Transformer and a threshold-based measure.
record.gate_note: The reported grokking-epoch means and the stated distribution comparison are results. The proposed explanations for why Muon helps and the cited results from other work are not this study's own experimental outcomes. Results are aggregated across tasks and softmax configurations; no per-task or per-softmax numerical results are stated.
record.test_reason: The study uses standard grokking tasks to compare optimizers and reports only the epoch at which validation accuracy reaches 95%. It never reports when training accuracy saturated, so the delay itself, and its dependence on training-set size, cannot be read. The optimizer effect bears on the timing of grokking but tests no version as stated. On V7, Muon shortens time to the threshold, but nothing shows the delay disappearing. Softmax and stablemax effects, the V7-relevant control, are not reported separately.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that Muon significantly accelerates grokking relative to AdamW. They attribute this, without testing it, to Muon's update geometry (spectral norm constraints, second-order cues) steering models away from memorization.
record.recipe_differences: Uses small algorithmic tasks and training/validation splits, but tests a modern Transformer, compares Muon with AdamW and several softmax variants, and defines grokking by reaching validation accuracy ≥95% after training accuracy stabilizes near 100%. The original method's exact recipe is not stated in this text.
record.method_sensitivity: Optimizer choice changes the aggregate mean epoch to the grokking threshold. Softmax variants are included in the experiments, but their separate effects are not reported.

fits_no_version.finding: Pooled across six or seven algorithmic tasks and three softmax variants, Muon reaches 95% validation accuracy at mean epoch 102.89 versus 153.09 for AdamW (t≈5.02, p≈6.3e-8). Muon also shows a tighter distribution.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Optimizer choice (Muon vs AdamW) shifts the time to grokking on algorithmic tasks, with weight decay held equal.

record.problems: The text reports aggregate results rather than task- or softmax-specific results, and does not give the full accuracy trajectories or uncertainty intervals for the means. It says there are seven numerical tasks, while the task overview lists six.
record.rows_left_out: No separately reported task- or softmax-specific outcomes are provided in the text to extract as additional rows.

untested.parts: Chance-level validation accuracy before the jump; the size of the delay after training saturates; dependence of the delay on training-set size. Split fractions differ by task, but no comparison across sizes is reported.

Whether the delay vanishes under controlled optimizer or numerical choices. Stablemax and sparsemax were run, but their results are not reported separately, and Muon only shortens time to the threshold.
Not tested; weight decay is held equal across optimizers.

missing.what: Epoch at which training accuracy saturated, per optimizer. This is needed to measure the delay.
missing.locator: Not reported; Experimental Results gives only threshold epochs

missing.what: Per-softmax-variant results (softmax vs stablemax vs sparsemax). These are relevant to the numerical-stability artifact account.
missing.locator: Section 2.2 describes the variants; no results are reported

missing.what: Per-task results, number of seeds, and whether any runs failed to grok.
missing.locator: Section 2.4 and Experimental Results; not reported

record.verdict_notes: Very short preprint with pooled results only. The abstract says seven tasks, but the task table lists six. Reference 1 attributes the original grokking paper to the wrong authors. The mechanisms in Figure 1 are hypotheses, not results. The split fractions vary by task (50–80%), so they cannot be used to assess dependence on dataset size.

versions.untested_parts: The study defines grokking as reaching at least 95% validation accuracy after training accuracy has stabilized near 100%, but does not report the full chance-to-near-perfect trajectory. It does not compare training-set sizes for the same task, so whether the delay grows as the training set shrinks is untested.
No circuit formation, memorizing-component removal, or continuous mechanism progress measure is reported.
The tasks are algorithmic; no non-algorithmic data, initialization-scale sweep, weight-norm sweep, or lazy-to-rich transition is tested.
No LLM pretraining or realistic-data fine-tuning is tested.
Weight decay strengths are held equivalent between optimizers; the study does not test the efficiency account, critical dataset size, or ungrokking below it.
The study does not identify or compare algorithms learned across runs.

Although softmax variants and optimizers are varied, the reported results do not establish that grokking is an optimizer or numerical artifact, or test whether it disappears when such factors are controlled.

rows.measure: Mean epoch to validation accuracy ≥95%, after training accuracy stabilized near 100%
rows.uncertainty: Two-sample comparison with Muon: t ≈ 5.0175; p ≈ 6.33 × 10−8
rows.note: The study reports this as an aggregate mean across experimental conditions, not a task-specific result. Its operational definition ties the threshold to prior stabilization of training accuracy.
rows.check: This is the AdamW mean epoch to 95% validation accuracy, pooled across tasks, softmax variants and seeds. No training-saturation epoch is given, so the gap between memorization and generalization, which is what V1 names, cannot be read. The 'observed' state is not supported.
